name: Mungpoo
tagline: Tagore's hill retreat among India's first cinchona plantation
meta_description: Mungpoo on a budget: Tagore's house (Rabindra Bhavan), Maitreyi Devi, the 1864 cinchona plantation, how to get there, what it costs and when to go.
summary: Mungpoo (Mangpu) is a plantation village of about 1,100–1,200 m, roughly 33 km from Darjeeling, built around India's first government cinchona plantation, begun in 1864. Rabindranath Tagore stayed here four times between 1938 and 1940 with Maitreyi Devi; the house is now Rabindra Bhavan, a small museum. A quiet, inexpensive day trip or overnight.

local_story.title: Quinine, a chemist's house and Tagore's last summers
paras: Mungpoo was shaped by a fever. Malaria killed and disabled huge numbers of people in British India, and the only effective remedy was quinine, extracted from the bark of the South American cinchona tree. In 1864 the government began planting cinchona on these warm, wet slopes above the Teesta valley, the first such plantation in India. A quinine factory followed, and Mungpoo grew into a company village of plantation workers, chemists and managers. The plantation still runs today under the West Bengal Directorate of Cinchona and Other Medicinal Plants.

In the late 1930s the chemist in charge at the factory was Dr Manmohan Sen, whose wife, Maitreyi Devi, was a writer who had known Rabindranath Tagore since childhood. At her invitation the ageing poet came to stay: from 21 May 1938 into June; again from 14 May to 17 June 1939; from 12 September to early November 1939; and from 21 April 1940, when his 79th birthday was celebrated in Mungpoo. He wrote, painted and talked late into the evenings in the bungalow.

Maitreyi Devi later wrote about those stays in Mongpute Rabindranath, published in English as Tagore by the Fireside. She is also remembered for Na Hanyate (1974), her answer to Mircea Eliade's novel Bengal Nights. The house where Tagore stayed is now Rabindra Bhavan, a small museum of his furniture, photographs, paintings and letters, and every year around 25 Baishakh, in early May, Mungpoo marks his birth anniversary. Few hill villages hold so much of one writer's life in so few rooms.

did_you_know: India's first government cinchona plantation was started at Mungpoo in 1864 to produce quinine against malaria; it is still run by West Bengal's Directorate of Cinchona and Other Medicinal Plants.
Rabindranath Tagore stayed at Mungpoo four times between May 1938 and 1940, and his 79th birthday was celebrated there in 1940.
Maitreyi Devi, Tagore's host at Mungpoo, wrote Mongpute Rabindranath about his stays, and in 1974 published Na Hanyate in reply to Mircea Eliade's novel Bengal Nights.
intro: Mungpoo is a village for readers, and for anyone curious about how the hills were really used under the British. There are no big viewpoints or bazaars here. Instead you find slopes of cinchona and other medicinal plants, the long sheds and chimneys of a government factory, rows of workers' quarters, and, in a garden on the hillside, the bungalow where Tagore spent four of the last summers and autumns of his life. It is warmer than Darjeeling, green, and very quiet once the factory shift has changed.

Most visitors come for a few hours: Rabindra Bhavan, a walk on the plantation roads and lunch. We suggest reading a little Tagore, or Maitreyi Devi's account of his stays, before you go; it turns a small museum into a moving visit. The museum has closed for repairs at times, and opening hours vary, so check current status before you travel. If you can, come in early May, when the village marks his birth anniversary.

highlights.title: Rabindra Bhavan
highlights.text: The bungalow where Tagore stayed with Maitreyi Devi and Dr Manmohan Sen between 1938 and 1940, now a small museum. Rooms keep his furniture, photographs, some of his paintings and letters. Allow an hour, read the captions slowly, and check opening status before you go.

highlights.title: The 1864 cinchona plantation
highlights.text: Slopes of cinchona trees, whose bark yielded quinine, cover the hills around the village. The plantation, begun in 1864, was the first in India and is still run by the state's Directorate of Cinchona and Other Medicinal Plants. Walk the plantation roads for a sense of its scale.

highlights.title: The quinine factory village
highlights.text: Long factory sheds, offices and workers' lines give Mungpoo the feel of an old company town. Factory visits are not a routine tourist service, but the village around it, with its quarters, schools and small shops, tells the story of the plantation on its own.

highlights.title: Rabindra Jayanti in early May
highlights.text: Every year around 25 Baishakh, Tagore's birth anniversary in the Bengali calendar, Mungpoo marks the day at Rabindra Bhavan with songs and readings. It is a small, local occasion and a good reason to plan a visit in early May.

highlights.title: Maitreyi Devi's story
highlights.text: Read Tagore by the Fireside, Maitreyi Devi's account of the poet's stays, before you come. She is also the author of Na Hanyate, her reply to Mircea Eliade's Bengal Nights. Her house is the heart of Mungpoo's story.

highlights.title: Warm, quiet slopes
highlights.text: At about 1,100–1,200 m Mungpoo is milder than Darjeeling, green and almost free of tourist traffic. It is a gentle stop for older travellers and families, with short walks rather than steep climbs. Bring a book and sit in the sun.

how_to_reach.text: The simplest way. Mungpoo is about 33 km from Darjeeling by hill roads, roughly 1.5–2 hours each way. A car for the day costs about ₹3,000–4,000. Ask the driver to combine it with Takdah, Tinchuley or the Peshok road if you have time, and check road conditions after rain.

From Siliguri or NJP, roads run via Sevoke and up NH10 along the Teesta to Rambi, then climb to Mungpoo. A reserved car costs roughly ₹2,500–3,500. NH10 has had long closures and damage since the October 2023 Teesta flood, so check current status before you travel; drivers may route another way.

Shared jeeps serve Mungpoo for local people, but services are few and timings change; fares are roughly ₹150–250 a seat. Ask at the jeep stands in Siliguri or Darjeeling the day before. For a short visit with a museum stop, a reserved car is usually worth the extra cost.

where_to_stay: We do not name individual properties in Mungpoo, as we cannot vouch for them. Most visitors come on a day trip from Darjeeling, or stop on the way between Siliguri and Darjeeling. If you want to stay, a few family homestays in Mungpoo village and the plantation settlements around it offer simple rooms at about ₹1,500–2,200 per person with dinner and breakfast. Book through a Darjeeling agent or by phone in advance, especially around Rabindra Jayanti in early May. Takdah and Tinchuley, not far away, have more homestay choice.
tips: Check whether Rabindra Bhavan is open, and its hours, before you set out; it has closed for repairs at times.
Read Maitreyi Devi's Tagore by the Fireside or a few Tagore poems first; the museum is small and the context matters.
Stay on public roads in the plantation and ask before photographing the factory or workers.
Check the status of NH10 and the Rambi road if you are coming up from Siliguri.
Carry cash; Mungpoo has few shops and card payments are rare.

experiences.title: Rabindra Bhavan, Tagore's house at Mungpoo
experiences.summary: Visit the bungalow where Rabindranath Tagore stayed four times between 1938 and 1940 as the guest of Maitreyi Devi. A small museum of his furniture, photographs, paintings and letters, in a quiet garden among the cinchona slopes.
body: The house belonged to the cinchona plantation and was the home of Dr Manmohan Sen, the chemist in charge at the quinine factory, and his wife, the writer Maitreyi Devi. Tagore came to stay at her invitation in May 1938 and returned three times, the last from 21 April 1940, when his 79th birthday was celebrated here. These were among the last journeys of a poet who died in August 1941.

Today the bungalow is Rabindra Bhavan, a small museum. The rooms keep pieces of the furniture he used, photographs from his stays, some of his paintings and letters. It is not a grand museum, and that is part of its charm: you can stand in the rooms where he worked and look out at the same green slopes. Spend a few minutes in the garden as well; the view across the slopes is much as he would have seen it, and the stillness explains why he came back.

The house has been under repair at times, and opening days and hours vary. Check current status before you travel, ideally through a Darjeeling agent or your driver. Read Maitreyi Devi's Tagore by the Fireside beforehand; she describes these rooms, the evenings and the conversations in detail. Photography rules inside can vary, so ask the caretaker before you take pictures, keep voices low in the rooms, and sign the visitors' book if there is one.

faqs.q: Why did Tagore stay in Mungpoo?
faqs.a: He came at the invitation of Maitreyi Devi, a writer he had known since her childhood, whose husband Dr Manmohan Sen was the chemist in charge at Mungpoo's quinine factory. The quiet, mild hill climate suited the ageing poet. He stayed four times between May 1938 and 1940.

faqs.q: What is there to see at Rabindra Bhavan?
faqs.a: The rooms where Tagore stayed, with furniture he used, photographs from his visits, some of his paintings and letters. It is a small museum and takes about an hour. The setting, a hill bungalow in a garden among cinchona slopes, is as much part of the visit as the exhibits.

faqs.q: Is Rabindra Bhavan open every day?
faqs.a: Opening days and hours vary, and the museum has closed for repair work at times. Do not assume it will be open on a public holiday or late in the afternoon. Check current status before you travel, through your driver, a Darjeeling agent or local contacts in Mungpoo.

experiences.title: Walk the 1864 cinchona plantation
experiences.summary: Walk the plantation roads of India's first cinchona plantation, begun in 1864 to make quinine against malaria. Old factory sheds, workers' lines and slopes of medicinal trees tell a story of empire, disease and science.
body: For much of the 19th century malaria was one of the great killers in India, and quinine, from the bark of the South American cinchona tree, was the only effective treatment. The government's answer was to grow it here. Cinchona planting at Mungpoo began in 1864, the first such plantation in India, and a quinine factory followed. The estate is still run by the West Bengal Directorate of Cinchona and Other Medicinal Plants.

Walk the public roads through the plantation and around the village. You will pass slopes of cinchona trees, nurseries, factory buildings and long lines of workers' quarters, many of them home to families who have worked here for generations. The land is warm and green, and the roads are gentle by hill standards. Cinchona trees are evergreen, with glossy leaves and, in season, clusters of small pale, scented flowers; ask a worker to point one out if you are not sure.

Factory visits are not a routine tourist service and may need permission from the directorate, so do not expect to go inside. Stay on public roads, ask before photographing buildings or people, and do not pick plants or strip bark. Combine the walk with Rabindra Bhavan for a half day. Afternoons can bring mist and rain, so go in the morning, wear shoes with grip for the steeper side lanes and carry water, as shops are few.

faqs.q: Can I visit the quinine factory in Mungpoo?
faqs.a: Not as a routine. The factory is a working government unit under the Directorate of Cinchona and Other Medicinal Plants, and visits may need prior permission. Walking the public roads through the plantation and village is usually fine. Ask locally and check current status before you travel if a factory visit matters to you.

faqs.q: When was the Mungpoo cinchona plantation started?
faqs.a: Cinchona planting at Mungpoo began in 1864, making it the first government cinchona plantation in India. It was set up to produce quinine, the main treatment for malaria at the time, and a quinine factory followed. The plantation is still run by the West Bengal Directorate of Cinchona and Other Medicinal Plants.

faqs.q: Is quinine still made at Mungpoo?
faqs.a: The plantation and factory still operate under the state's cinchona directorate, though synthetic antimalarials have long replaced bark quinine for most uses, and the directorate also works with other medicinal plants. Ask locally for what is produced now; output and activities have changed over the decades.

experiences.title: Tagore's birth anniversary in early May
experiences.summary: Come to Mungpoo around 25 Baishakh, Tagore's birth anniversary in the Bengali calendar, when the village marks the day at Rabindra Bhavan with songs and readings. A small, local occasion in the house where his 79th birthday was celebrated.
body: Rabindranath Tagore was born on 25 Baishakh in the Bengali calendar, which falls in early May. Across Bengal the day is marked as Rabindra Jayanti with his songs, poems and plays. In Mungpoo it carries extra weight: in 1940 his own 79th birthday was celebrated here, in the house that is now Rabindra Bhavan. Schools, cultural groups and families across the state sing Rabindrasangeet, his songs, through the day. For a Tagore reader, there is no better place to spend it in the hills.

Each year the village marks the anniversary at the museum, usually with songs, recitations and local participation. Programmes vary from year to year and are modest, so do not expect a festival ground; expect a few hours of Tagore's songs in the place he chose for some of his last summers. Visitors are generally welcome to listen quietly; sit at the back, keep phones silent, and follow the lead of local organisers on where to stand and when to take photographs.

Early May is also a pleasant time in Mungpoo, warm by day and green before the monsoon. Rooms in the few homestays fill around the date, and visitors come up from Darjeeling and Siliguri. Book ahead, confirm the date and programme locally, and check current status before you travel. Walk the plantation roads in the cool of the morning, before the programme begins, and plan your drive back to Darjeeling or Siliguri in daylight.

faqs.q: When is Rabindra Jayanti celebrated in Mungpoo?
faqs.a: On or around 25 Baishakh in the Bengali calendar, Tagore's birth anniversary, which falls in early May, usually 8 or 9 May. The exact date and programme at Rabindra Bhavan vary year to year, so confirm locally before you plan. Check current status before you travel.

faqs.q: What happens on Rabindra Jayanti at Rabindra Bhavan?
faqs.a: The anniversary is usually marked with Tagore's songs, recitations of his poems and tributes at the house where he stayed. It is a modest, local occasion rather than a large festival. The programme changes from year to year, so go for the atmosphere rather than a fixed schedule.

faqs.q: Is early May a good time to visit Mungpoo?
faqs.a: Yes. Days are warm and the slopes green, with clear spells before the monsoon arrives in June. It is the busiest time for Mungpoo's few homestays because of Rabindra Jayanti, so book ahead. Expect haze over the valleys and afternoon showers in some years.

experiences.title: Climb from the Teesta at Rambi to Mungpoo
experiences.summary: Leave the Teesta valley road at Rambi and climb through warm forest and cinchona slopes to Mungpoo. A quieter way into the Darjeeling hills from Siliguri, with the river far below and the plantation village at the top.
body: From Siliguri the road follows the Teesta upstream from Sevoke through a deep, forested gorge. At Rambi, a small bazaar on NH10, a road turns off and climbs to Mungpoo, leaving the river behind as it gains height through mixed forest, farms and, higher up, the cinchona slopes. It is a quieter way into the hills than the busy Hill Cart Road through Kurseong. The change from the hot riverbank to the cooler slopes takes well under an hour.

Go in the morning for the clearest views over the gorge, and stop for tea at Rambi before the climb. Once at Mungpoo, visit Rabindra Bhavan and the plantation, and either return the same way or carry on towards Darjeeling by the hill roads with your driver. Watch the vegetation change as you climb: sal and broadleaf forest near the river give way to farm terraces and then to the darker green of the plantation.

NH10 along the Teesta has suffered repeated landslides and serious damage since the October 2023 flood, with long closures. This route depends on its condition. Ask your driver, check current status before you travel and be ready to come in via Darjeeling instead. From October to April the road is usually at its best, though repair works can still cause waits of an hour or more. Carry water and snacks.

faqs.q: How do I get to Mungpoo from Siliguri?
faqs.a: The direct route runs from Siliguri via Sevoke along NH10 beside the Teesta to Rambi, then climbs to Mungpoo, roughly 2.5–3 hours by car for ₹2,500–3,500. Because NH10 has had long closures since October 2023, drivers sometimes go via Darjeeling instead. Check current status before you travel.

faqs.q: Is NH10 open to Rambi?
faqs.a: It changes. Since the October 2023 Teesta flood, NH10 between Sevoke and Rangpo has had repeated landslides, damage and closures, sometimes for weeks. Ask your driver or local contacts on the day, follow traffic updates from the district administration and check current status before you travel.

faqs.q: Can I visit Mungpoo on the way from Siliguri to Darjeeling?
faqs.a: Yes, if roads allow. Go up via Rambi to Mungpoo, see Rabindra Bhavan and the plantation, then continue to Darjeeling by hill roads with a reserved car. It turns a 3-hour transfer into a full day. Start early, and check road conditions on both legs before you leave.

faqs.q: Where is Mungpoo?
faqs.a: Mungpoo (also spelt Mangpu or Mongpoo) is a plantation village in Darjeeling district, about 33 km from Darjeeling, above the Teesta valley near Rambi on NH10. It sits at roughly 1,100–1,200 m, so it is milder than Darjeeling. It is best known for its cinchona plantation and Tagore's house.

faqs.q: Why is Mungpoo famous?
faqs.a: For two reasons: India's first government cinchona plantation, begun in 1864 to make quinine against malaria, and Rabindranath Tagore's four stays between 1938 and 1940 with Maitreyi Devi. The house where he stayed is now Rabindra Bhavan, a small museum of his furniture, photographs, paintings and letters.

faqs.q: How do I reach Mungpoo from Darjeeling?
faqs.a: By reserved car, about 33 km and 1.5–2 hours each way by hill roads; a day trip costs about ₹3,000–4,000. Shared jeeps serve the village for local people but are infrequent, so ask at the Darjeeling stand the day before if you want to try. Check road conditions after rain.

faqs.q: Is Rabindra Bhavan in Mungpoo open now?
faqs.a: It has been open to visitors in recent years but has closed for repairs at times, and opening days and hours vary. Check current status before you travel through your driver or a Darjeeling agent. Avoid arriving late in the afternoon, when you may find it closing.

faqs.q: How many times did Tagore visit Mungpoo?
faqs.a: Four times: from 21 May 1938 into June; 14 May to 17 June 1939; 12 September to early November 1939; and from 21 April 1940, when his 79th birthday was celebrated there. He stayed with Maitreyi Devi and her husband, Dr Manmohan Sen, chemist at the quinine factory.

faqs.q: Who was Maitreyi Devi?
faqs.a: A Bengali writer and poet who knew Tagore from her childhood and was his host at Mungpoo, where her husband was the chemist in charge at the quinine factory. She wrote Mongpute Rabindranath (Tagore by the Fireside) about his stays, and Na Hanyate (1974), her reply to Mircea Eliade's novel Bengal Nights.

faqs.q: Is Mungpoo worth a day trip?
faqs.a: Yes, for anyone interested in Tagore, Bengali literature or the history of the hills. The museum, the plantation roads and the quiet village make a good half day. If you only want mountain views and cafés, it will feel slow; combine it with Takdah or the Peshok road.

faqs.q: Can I stay overnight in Mungpoo?
faqs.a: Yes, a few family homestays in and around the village offer simple rooms at about ₹1,500–2,200 per person with dinner and breakfast. We do not name them as we cannot vouch for individual properties. Book ahead, especially around Rabindra Jayanti in early May; Takdah and Tinchuley have more choice.

faqs.q: What is the best time to visit Mungpoo?
faqs.a: October to May. Autumn and winter are dry with clear valley views and mild days; early May brings Rabindra Jayanti at the museum. Avoid July and August, when heavy rain, leeches and landslides on the Teesta valley roads make the trip slow and risky.
